description:
We are a creative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our project, Dancing with the Sars, aims to bring science and creativity together in an engaging and innovative way.

We welcome curious, motivated people who enjoy brainstorming ideas and solving problems to build something meaningful. We are looking for teammates with skills in coding, data analysis, scientific research. 

Join North Stars and let’s turn our ideas into something extraordinary!
summary: EarthWake: Azuero Shaken is an interactive web story that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data to reveal how the magnitude 7.7 earthquake of October 9, 2026 changed the Azuero Peninsula in Panama. We compared NISAR GCOV images from July and October 2026 with before-and-after sliders and a change map, and measured the variation in two sectors of the peninsula. Because the rainy season also alters the radar signal, we added NISAR GUNW interferograms from two 12-day periods: before the earthquake, the color bands are straight and regular; after it, they bend and converge, revealing the ground movement caused by the earthquake. The page explains each image in simple terms, proposes the physical drivers behind the changes, and shows how free NISAR data, available every 12 days, could help communities and authorities monitor landslides, flooding and coastal subsidence, and decide where to inspect and rebuild more safely.
details:
What it does
EarthWake: Azuero Shaken is an interactive web story that shows how the magnitude 7.7 earthquake of October 9, 2026 changed the Azuero Peninsula in Panama, using radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite. Visitors drag a slider to compare radar images, explore a change map, and read a short explanation of each image: what it is, what to look for, and why it matters.

How it works
We downloaded NISAR GCOV products for July and October 2026 and processed them in ArcGIS Pro. We displayed the Frequency A radar layer with a stretched color scale, computed a change raster (Difference method) between both dates, and extracted statistics for the northern and southern sectors of the peninsula. The southern sector showed about 60% more variation. Because the rainy season also changes the radar signal, we added two NISAR GUNW interferograms from the same orbit track: September 20 to October 2 and October 2 to October 14. Before the earthquake, the color bands are straight and regular; after it, they bend and converge around one zone, revealing real ground movement.

Benefits and intended impact
NISAR data is free and revisits the same area every 12 days, through clouds, day and night. This approach can help civil protection agencies, scientists and local communities identify where the ground changed, monitor landslides, flooding and coastal subsidence, and decide where to inspect and rebuild more safely. It can be repeated for any future earthquake.

Tools
NASA Earthdata and ASF Vertex (data search and download), Esri ArcGIS Pro (processing and change detection), HTML, CSS and JavaScript (website), Python with OpenCV (aligning images for comparison), and GitHub Pages (hosting).

Creativity
The story is designed as a journey through space: a starry sky, northern lights and a north star, the symbol of our team NORTHSTARS, which visitors drag to compare images. Instead of only presenting results, the page invites the reader to question them and proposes hypotheses for what the radar shows.

Factors we considered
Scientific honesty: we explain that GCOV changes mix several causes (the earthquake, seasonal rain, vegetation and viewing angles) and use interferometry to isolate the earthquake signal. We also considered accessibility (plain language, mobile-friendly design, no software needed) and local relevance, since the earthquake affected our own country.
